# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira and considering switching to Plane, likely due to Plane's self-hosted and free option. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch to take advantage of Plane's cost savings and data ownership.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Plane is free and self-hosted, while Jira has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Plane allows users to host their own data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively straightforward.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane uses third-party plugins for Git integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Robust feature set
* Native integration with Git
* Large user community
* Scalable for large teams
* Mobile apps available
* Limited customization options
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Data ownership and control
* Simple setup process
* Customizable
* Limited native integrations
* Limited scalability

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a robust feature set and native integration with Git. It is also a good option for teams that need a high level of scalability and are willing to pay for it. Plane, on the other hand, is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that want a free and self-hosted solution with data ownership and control. It is also a good option for teams that value simplicity and customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use a third-party import tool to convert the data to Plane's format.
3. Set up a new Plane instance and configure the necessary plugins and integrations.
4. Import the converted data into Plane.
5. Test and verify that all data has been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited native integrations and scalability issues. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's API is still in development, which may limit its customization options. However, for small to medium-sized teams that value data ownership and control, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira, and we recommend considering it as an option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need native Git integration
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that want to save on costs
* Teams that require data ownership and control
* Teams with simple project management needs
* Teams that are already self-hosting other tools and want to add Plane to their infrastructure

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. However, users will need to cover their own server costs.
### Can I migrate from Jira to Plane?
Yes, it is possible to migrate from Jira to Plane using third-party import tools.
### Is Plane scalable?
Plane is not yet scalable for large teams and enterprises. It is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
### Does Plane have native integration with Git?
No, Plane does not have native integration with Git. However, it uses third-party plugins for Git integration.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet. Plane is still in development and has some technical limitations.

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are project management tools used for organizing and tracking tasks. Both tools benefit teams and individuals looking for a flexible and customizable way to manage their work. The core use case for both tools is to provide a Kanban-style board for visualizing workflows, and a key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Trello has a more user-friendly and intuitive interface, making it easier to set up and start using, while WeKan requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to handle large teams and enterprises, while WeKan is better suited for smaller teams or individuals who want more control over their data.
* Integration difference: Trello has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools and services, while WeKan has a more limited set of integrations due to its open-source nature.

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $250/month (50 users \* $5/user/month) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1000/month (200 users \* $5/user/month) | $0 (server cost only) |

**Trello:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and suitable for large teams and enterprises
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
**WeKan:**
* Completely free and open-source
* Allows for self-hosting and full control over data ownership
* Highly customizable and flexible
* Limited integrations with third-party tools

Trello is a good choice for teams of all sizes who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party tools. It is particularly well-suited for large teams and enterprises who need a scalable solution. WeKan, on the other hand, is a good choice for smaller teams or individuals who want full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting and technical setup. It is also a good option for those who prioritize data ownership and customization.

## Migration Path

2. Set up a self-hosted WeKan instance on your server or use a cloud hosting service.
3. Use the WeKan import tool to import your Trello data into WeKan.
4. Configure your WeKan instance and customize it to your needs.
5. Test and verify that all your data has been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to self-host and set up. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's integration with third-party tools is limited compared to Trello. However, for teams who prioritize data ownership and customization, WeKan is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Trello to WeKan if you are a small team or individual with basic project management needs and do not require a wide range of integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who prioritize data ownership and customization
* Individuals who want full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting
* Teams who do not require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools

### Can I integrate WeKan with other tools?

# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that cater to individuals and teams looking to store and share files. This comparison is beneficial for users who value data ownership and are considering switching from a proprietary service to a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is file storage and collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, especially for large teams or organizations, since it can be self-hosted on premises or in a private cloud.
* Integration with ONLYOFFICE: Nextcloud has a built-in integration with ONLYOFFICE for document editing, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of third-party integrations
* Robust file sharing and collaboration features
* Reliable and fast file syncing
* Limited control over data ownership and security
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* High scalability and customization
* Integrated document editing with ONLYOFFICE
* Free to use with self-hosting
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's ideal for teams that need a straightforward, user-friendly solution for file storage and sharing. On the other hand, Nextcloud is a better choice for larger teams or organizations that value data ownership and scalability. It's also suitable for teams with technical expertise who can handle the setup and management of a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance on your own server or use a hosted service.
3. Import your exported data into Nextcloud using the WebDAV protocol or a compatible import tool.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it's essential to note that Nextcloud's self-hosting requirement can be a limitation for teams without technical expertise. For users who value ease of use and don't require full control over their data, Dropbox might still be the better choice. 

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need advanced collaboration features
* Individuals who value data ownership and security
* Teams with technical expertise who can handle self-hosting
* Organizations with large storage needs and scalability requirements
* Users who don't need seamless integration with Microsoft Office

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting. You'll need to cover the cost of server maintenance and upkeep, but there are no per-user fees.

### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers more control over data security and encryption, but both solutions have robust security measures in place. The security of your data ultimately depends on your specific setup and configuration.

### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other tools and services?
Yes, Nextcloud has a wide range of integrations with third-party tools and services, including ONLYOFFICE, Collabora, and more.

### How do I migrate my data from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
You can export your Dropbox data using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool, then import it into Nextcloud using the WebDAV protocol or a compatible import tool.

### Is Nextcloud suitable for large teams?
Yes, Nextcloud is highly scalable and can handle large teams and organizations. It's ideal for teams with technical expertise who can handle the setup and management of a self-hosted solution.

# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Google Workspace and Nextcloud are two popular tools for team collaboration and productivity. Both offer a range of features, including document management, email, and calendar sharing, but they differ significantly in terms of cost, data ownership, and setup complexity. The core use case for both tools is to provide a centralized platform for teams to work together, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Google Workspace charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Google Workspace stores data on its servers, while Nextcloud allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* Setup complexity: Google Workspace is generally easier to set up, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Google Workspace is more scalable, with better support for large teams, while Nextcloud can be more challenging to scale.
* Integration: Google Workspace has better integration with other Google tools, such as Google Drive and Google Docs, while Nextcloud has better integration with other open-source tools, such as OnlyOffice.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $300-$900/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,200-$3,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Google Workspace:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Well-integrated with other Google tools
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data
**Nextcloud:**
* Free and self-hosted
* High level of control over data
* Customizable and extensible
* Good security features
* Can be challenging to set up and scale

## When to Choose Each
Google Workspace is a good choice for teams that need a simple, easy-to-use collaboration platform and are willing to pay a monthly fee per user. It's particularly well-suited for small to medium-sized teams that already use other Google tools. Nextcloud, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that want a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers. It's particularly well-suited for large teams or organizations with complex security requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Google Workspace in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Nextcloud server and configure it to meet your needs.
3. Use the Nextcloud import tool to import your data from Google Workspace.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with other tools.
5. Test your Nextcloud setup to ensure it's working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready alternative to Google Workspace for many users, offering a high level of control over data and customization options. However, it's worth noting that Nextcloud can be challenging to set up and scale, particularly for large teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's calendar and contact management features are not as robust as those offered by Google Workspace. Overall, we recommend Nextcloud for teams that value data sovereignty and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced collaboration features
* Teams that require a high level of control over their data
* Organizations with complex security requirements
* Teams that are already using other open-source tools
* Individuals who want a self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud with my existing Google account?
No, Nextcloud requires you to create a new account or use an existing LDAP or Active Directory setup.
### Is Nextcloud compatible with all file types?
Yes, Nextcloud supports a wide range of file types, including documents, images, and videos.
### Can I access Nextcloud from my mobile device?
Yes, Nextcloud has mobile apps for Android and iOS.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Google Workspace?
Nextcloud offers a high level of security, but its security depends on how it's set up and configured.
### Can I migrate my Google Drive files to Nextcloud?
Yes, you can use the Nextcloud import tool to migrate your Google Drive files.

# Monday.com vs Plane

## Overview

Visual work management platform used by 180,000+ organizations. is a popular proprietary tool in the project-management space. Plane is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Monday.com costs $9-$19/user/month; Plane is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Monday.com is Proprietary; Plane is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Plane can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Plane eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Plane has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Monday.com | Plane |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $9-$19/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$450/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,800/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Monday.com

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Plane

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [makeplane/plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) * ~31k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Monday.com if:** Monday.com is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Plane if:** Plane is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Monday.com in its standard export format, review Plane import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Plane is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Monday.com tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Plane instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Monday.com, switching to self-hosted Plane will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Monday.com until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Monday.com paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Plane free to use?
Yes. Plane is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Monday.com to Plane?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Monday.com data, follow the Plane import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Plane get regular updates?
Yes. Plane has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Plane without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Plane development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Monday.com](https://monday.com) and [Plane](https://plane.so) before making decisions.*
